![](featured.jpg)

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
We take *[The Art of Painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Art_of_Painting)* from Johannes Vermeer, decouple it into three channels: luminance, red-green, and blue-yellow. We then spatially blur one of the channels while keeping the other two channels unchanged and then reconstruct the image. Evidently, our vision is much more sensitive to spatially blurring in the luminance channel (left) than is to blurring in the red-green channel (middle) and in the blue-yellow channel (left).
Interestingly, this also shows that the Magnocellular pathway, while is said to be responsible for the dark-light opponent cells, cannot alone be exclusively responsible for our luminance perception (see [why here](https://learnvisualcomputing.github.io/hvs-color.html#m-pathway-does-not-fully-account-for-luminance)).
:::

We live in and experience [an immense world](https://edyong.me/an-immense-world).
A big part of our experience is made possible through our visual system: the eyes, the retina, and the brain.
Understanding the human visual system (HVS) is important at two levels.
First and foremost, for the science itself --- for the [pleasure of finding things out](https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Pleasure_of_Finding_Things_Out/s6LzV_U6PskC?hl=en&gbpv=0).
As Edwin H. Land once put it, the true application of science is that “we finally know what we are doing.”
Second, many visual computing systems (such as smartphones, AR glasses, VR headsets, and image generation models) generate images that are ultimately consumed by humans, so understanding how the HVS processes and interprets these signals allows us to better engineer such systems.

Going beyond vision, how do humans generalize so easily to speakers with different accents, how does our immediate and past experience shape our memory, and, ultimately, why and how do we possess intelligence?
We are interested in fundamentally understanding human perception, cognition, and intelligence, and using the understanding to build better algorithms, systems, and agents.
